meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There is no limit to the amount of good you can do if you don't care who gets the credit'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Reagan's line. The saying is documented back to 1863; Reagan's desk plaque used different words. The popular wording is a modern paraphrase.

answer.label: Not Ronald Reagan’s words — a much older saying, in altered form
answer.authorName: Attributed to “Father Strickland,” an English Jesuit (earliest documented, 1863)
answer.sourceLine: The idea long predates Reagan. According to Quote Investigator, the earliest documented version appears in a diary entry dated 21 September 1863 (published 1897), which credits “Father Strickland”: “a man may do an immense deal of good, if he does not care who gets the credit for it.” Reagan did keep a plaque of the saying on his desk, but the Reagan Library records its wording as “There is no limit to what a man can do or where he can go if he doesn’t mind who gets the credit” — not the viral “amount of good…don’t care” phrasing.

source.excerpt: a man may do an immense deal of good, if he does not care who gets the credit for it.
trail: Long before Reagan. Quote Investigator traces the saying to an 1863 diary entry (published 1897) crediting “Father Strickland,” and through Benjamin Jowett, C. E. Montague and others — decades before Reagan was born.

Reagan used different words. The Ronald Reagan Presidential Library gives his desk plaque as “There is no limit to what a man can do or where he can go if he doesn’t mind who gets the credit” — not the “amount of good…don’t care” version pinned on him online.
Even Goodreads flags it. The popular Reagan wording is tagged “misattributed” in its own quote database.

source.rightsNote: The exact viral wording — “There is no limit to the amount of good you can do if you don’t care who gets the credit” — is an anonymous modern paraphrase with no identifiable first source, so no copyright status can be responsibly asserted. The underlying saying is far older: its earliest documented form dates to an 1863 diary entry published in 1897 (public domain), and Reagan’s own desk-plaque wording differs again.

author.heading: About “Father Strickland” (earliest documented)
author.bio: Per Quote Investigator, the earliest documented form of this saying appears in Sir M. E. Grant Duff’s Notes from a Diary, in an entry dated 21 September 1863 that credits a Jesuit “Father Strickland” with the remark. The thought was already a proverbial commonplace by the late 1800s and was later echoed by Benjamin Jowett, Edward Everett Hale, C. E. Montague and others — long before Ronald Reagan adopted a version of it for his desk plaque.

misattribution.heading: How Reagan got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a classic “magnet name” case: an old, ownerless proverb about not seeking credit gets pinned on a famous modern figure — and the wording drifts in the process.

items.why: The line is universally credited to Reagan online, but he did not originate it and did not use this exact phrasing. The Reagan Library records his desk plaque as “There is no limit to what a man can do or where he can go if he doesn’t mind who gets the credit.” The viral “amount of good…don’t care” version is a later mutation. Goodreads even tags the Reagan attribution “misattributed.”

Quote Investigator notes a 1988 attribution to Truman for which it found no solid support, and an early attribution to Oxford’s Benjamin Jowett that was itself reassigned to “a Jesuit Father” by 1909.

misattribution.truthLine: The saying is documented back to 1863 — before Reagan was born — and the earliest source credits an English Jesuit, not any president, per Quote Investigator.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The sentiment is genuinely old and genuinely ownerless. By the late 19th century, “never mind who gets the credit” was already circulating as a proverb, attached at various points to a Jesuit priest, to Oxford’s Benjamin Jowett, and to the American clergyman Edward Everett Hale. No single author can claim it.

Reagan’s role was to popularize it, not to write it. He kept a plaque bearing a version of the saying on his desk as Governor of California and as President — but with the words “what a man can do or where he can go.” The internet later smoothed that into “the amount of good you can do,” and dropped the older phrasing entirely, leaving a quote that is neither Reagan’s wording nor Reagan’s invention.
context.pull: Documented in 1863 — and even Reagan’s own plaque used different words.
